rv.q: And I defy anyone not to shiver when this Cyrano, in the play’s penultimate scene, stands tall amid cannon and musket smoke, his arms raised to the heavens.
This production may be a tad overdone, overstuffed and overwrought at times, but it has something that Cyrano himself considered one of the most important things in the world. It has panache.
Mr. Hodge's Cyrano is a passionate, tortured soul whose physical deformity has made him simultaneously bold and shy.
But while Hodge attacks the title role with formidable energy and inventiveness, his virtuosic display muffles the poetry of the play.
But a lack of restraint spoils the fun, making it all seem too big (Cyrano’s honker), too much (stomping on tables), and over the top (Douglas Hodge’s star turn).
Hodge is an enormous talent, and he does excellent work, but it does sometimes look like work.
It looks like a blunt instrument, a quality shared with this new Roundabout revival as a whole.
As staged by Jamie Lloyd, an English director making his Broadway debut,this "Cyrano" comes off as an irritating bore.

I suppose it’s possible that “Cyrano” traditionalists will not be as taken with Lloyd’s interpretation as I was. Nevertheless, I would urge everyone to check out Roundabout Theatre Company’s thoughtful, committed production.
Hodge's participation is largely why this presentation is a pleasure to watch, especially in the quicker, better-paced second act, where his pre-death monologue becomes the show's defining moment.
If not great or memorable, it's good, and very solid.
Hodge brings a rakish, roguish quality to the role that feels fresh.
If only they were enough to make up for this deflating misfire.
